la:adj:patrius.html:
pā^trĭus, a, um, adj.
pater
,
of or belonging to a father, fatherly, paternal (for syn. v paternus).
Lit.
In gen.: esse exitio rei patriae suae,: rem patriam et gloriam majorum foedare,: animus patrius,; ; : res patria atque avita,: potestas,; : jus et potestas,; : majestas,; : auctoritas,: amor,: benevolentia,: maeror,; : acerbitas,: monumentum,: amor,: arae. i. e. of Father Apollo, : patrium mimae donare fundum laremque, Hor S. 1, 2, 56: dolor pedum,hereditary,: ucerbitas, i. e. of his father, Liv 7, 5, 7: di patrii, of one's forefathers. like θεοι πατρῷοι, family gods, household gods, penates, , ; Hyg. ap. Macr S. 3, 4 fin.: hoc patrium est, potius consuefacere filium Suā sponte recte facere quam alieno metu, Ter Ad. 1, 1, 49.—Rarely, like paternus. = patris. patriā virtute praeditus filius, sepulchrum patrium, : poenas patrias persequi,: corpus patrium. ; : patrio instituto deditus studio litterarum,; : mos patrius et disciplina,: regnum patrium atque avitum,.—
In partic., in gram.: patrius casus,the genitive,; cf. patricus and paternus.—
Transf., in gen.
Handed down from one's forefathers, old-established, old, ancient (very rare): mos. hereditary, old-established custom, : leges. .—
Hereditary, innate, peculiar (poet.): praediscere patrios cultusque habitusque locorum,: patrius hic (pedum dolor) illi,the gout,. pavor genti, Sil 15, 722: adde, cruentis Quod patriura saevire Dahis,.—Hence,
Subst.
pā^trĭa, ae (old gen. patrial, ), f (sc. terra)
One's fatherland, native land or country, native place: erilis patria, salve,: eram imperator in patriā meā,: patria, quae communis est omnium nostrum parens. : omnes omnium caritates patria una complexa est.,: o pater, o patria, o Priami domus, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 118 Vahl.); cf.: o patria, o divum domus Ilium, Poët. ap. ; imitated by Verg. l. l.: o Romule, Romule die, Qualem te patriae custodem di genuerunt, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 116 Vahl.): patriā Atheniensis an Lacedaemonius,: Hispaniam sibi antiquam patriam esse, ap. .—
A dwelling-place, home: habuit alteram loci patriam, alteram juris,: Italiam quaero patriam,; cf. : exuere patriam,; cf. : patria major = μητρόπολις, the mother-city of colonists, .—Hence, prov.: patria est, ubicumque est bene, Poët. (prob. Pacuv.) ap. : quia propheta in suā patriā honorem non habet,; ; .—Poet. of things; Nilus, Qui patriam tantae tam bene celat aquae, the home, i. e. the source, : nimborum in patriam,: divisae arboribus patriae,; cf.: una atque eadem est vini patria atque magistri,. —*
pā^trĭum, ĭi, n. (sc. nomen), i. q. patronymicum, a patronymic, , 45.—*
Adv.: pā^trĭē, paternally: patrie monere,.

la:verb:patior.html:
pătĭor, passus, 3, v. dep. (
act. archaic collat. form patiunto, : patias, Naev. ap. P.) [cf. Greek ΠΑΘ, ΠΕΝΘ-, πέπονθα, πένθος], to bear, support, undergo, suffer, endure (syn.: fero, tolero).
Lit.
In gen.
Tu fortunatu's, ego miser: patiunda sunt,; : fortiter malum qui patitur, idem post potitur bonum, Ussing (al. patitur bonum): o passi graviora!; ; : belli injurias,: servitutem,: toleranter dolores pati,: gravissimum supplicium,: omnia saeva,: et facere et pati fortiter,: haec patienda censeo potius, quam, etc.,: Hannibal damnum haud aegerrime passus est,: exilium,: pauperiem,.

aliae nationes servitutem pati possunt, populi Romani propria est libertas, : extremam pati fortunam,: aequo animo magnum morbum pati,: mentietur in tormentis qui dolorem pati potest,: qui nec totam servitutem pati possunt, nec totam libertatem,: non potest generosus animus servitutem pati,: hiemem et aestatem juxta pati,.—

Absol.: dolor tristis res est . . . ad patiendum tolerandumque difficilis,; .—
To suffer, have, meet with, be visited or afflicted with (mostly postAug.): poenam,; ; ; : incommodum,: vim,: quicquid in captivum invenire potest, passurum te esse cogita,: mortem pati,; : indignam necem,: mortem,: rem modicam,: adversa proelia,: infamiam,: sterilitatem famemque,: cladem pati (post-Aug. for cladem accipere, etc.),; so, naufragium,: morbum,; : cruciatus corporis,: ultima,: injuriam,: ut is in culpā sit, qui faciat, non is qui patiatur injuriam,; cf.: de tribus unum esset optandum: aut facere injuriam nec accipere ... optimum est facere, impune si possis, secundum nec facere nec pati,.—
In partic.
In mal. part., to submit to another's lust, to prostitute one's self, ; cf. ; ; ; .—
To suffer, to pass a life of suffering or privation (poet.): certum est in silvis inter spelaea ferarum Malle pati,: novem cornix secula passa,; ; . —
Transf.
To suffer, bear, allow, permit, let (syn.: sino, permitto): illorum delicta,.—With acc. and inf.: neque tibi bene esse patere, et illis, quibus est, invides,; : siquidem potes pati esse te in lepido loco,: ista non modo homines, sed ne pecudes quidem passurae esse videntur,: nobiscum versari jam diutius non potes: non feram, non patiar, non sinam,: quantum illius ineuntis aetatis meae patiebatur pudor,: nullo se implicari negotio passus est,: duo spondei non fere se jungi patiuntur,: aut persuasurum se aut persuaderi sibi passurum,: ut vinci se consensu civitatis pateretur,; ; .—With acc.: neque enim dilationem pati tam vicinum bellum poterat,: recentis animi alter (consul) ... nullam dilationem patiebatur,.—With quin: non possum pati, Quin tibi caput demulceam,: nullum patiebatur esse diem, quin in foro diceret,.—Poet. with part.: nec plura querentem Passa,; (= passa queri, etc.).—Hence, facile, aequo animo pati, to be well pleased or content with, to acquiesce in, submit to: aegre, iniquo animo, moleste pati, to be displeased, offended, indignant at: quaeso aequo animo patitor,: apud me plus officii residere facillime patior,; : consilium meum a te probari ... facile patior,; : cum indigne pateretur nobilis mulier ... in conventum suam mimi filiam venisse,, § 31: periniquo patiebar animo, te a me digredi,; .—
To submit: patior quemvis durare laborem,: pro quo bis patiar mori,.—
To experience, undergo, to be in a certain state of mind or temper: nonne quiddam pati furori simile videatur,.—
In gram., to be passive, to have a passive sense: (verbum) cum haberet naturam patiendi,a passive nature,: modus patiendi,; .— Hence, pătĭens, entis, P. a., bearing, supporting, suffering, permitting.
Lit.: amnis navium patiens,i. e. navigable,: vomeris,: vetustatis,lasting, : equus patiens sessoris,.—
Transf.
That has the quality of enduring, patient: nimium patiens et lentus existimor,: animus,.—Comp.: meae quoque litterae te patientiorem lenioremque fecerunt,.—Sup.: patientissimae aures,: patientissimus exercitus,.—
That has the power of endurance, firm, unyielding, hard (poet.): patiens aratrum,: saxo patientior illa Sicano,.—Hence, adv.: pătĭenter, patiently: alterum patienter accipere, non repugnanter,: patienter et fortiter ferre aliquid,: patienter et aequo animo ferre difficultates,: prandere olus,.—Comp.: patientius alicujus potentiam ferre,.—Sup.: patientissime ferre aliquid,.

la:noun:pater.html:
păter, tris (old
gen PATRVS. Inscr Corp. Lat. 1469; dat PATRE, ib 182), m.
Sanscr. root pā, to nourish, protect; Lat. pasco; hence, Zend, patar, protector; Gr. πατηρ; Sanscr pitri; Engl. father; Germ. Vater
, a father, sire.
Lit.Aes. Ehem, pater mi, tu hic eras? De Tuus hercle vero et animo et patura pater, : patre certo nasci,: Servius Tullius captivā Corniculanā natus, patre nullo, matre servā,i. e. by an unknown father,: SI PATER FILIVM TER VENVM DVIT FILIVS A PATRE LIBER ESTO, Lex XII. Tab.: CORNELIVS SCIPIO BARBATVS GNAIVOD PATRE PROGNATVS, Epit. of the Scipios: ego a patre ita eram deductus,by my father,: aliquem patris loco colere debere,.—
Transf.
The father as head and rep resentative of the household, esp., paterfamilias and paterfamiliae: pauci milites patresque familiae recepti,: quemeunque patrem familiae arripuissetis,; v. familia.—
In plur.: patres, fathers, forefathers: patrum nostrorum aetas,: memoria patrum,: apud patres nostros,: patres majoresque nostri,: Dominus Deus patrum vestrorum, Vulg Exod 3, 15: descenderunt patres tui in Aegyptum,.—So in sing (eccl. Lat.): dixitque Jacob; Deus patris mei Abraham, etc.,: quod juravit ad Abra.

ham patrem nostrūm, .—

PATRES for parentes, parents, ; ; ; 704, 1.—
As a title of honor, father.—Of a deity, esp. of Jupiter: divum pater atque hominum rex, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 179 Vahl.); cf.: pater optime Olimpi, id. ap. (Ann. v. 198 ib.): ipse pater mediā nimborum in nocte coruscā Fulmina molitur dextrā,: Gradivumque patrem Geticis qui praesidet arvis,: pater Lemnius,i. e. Vulcan,: Bacche pater,; cf. Lenaeus,i. e. Bacchus,: pater Silvane,: Quirine pater, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 121 Vahl.): pater Tiberine, id. ap. (Ann. v. 55 ib.); of the Tiber, : Apenninus, Wagner: pater Aeneas,.—Of the creative or generative powers of nature as deities: pater Aether,: aequoreus, i. e. Ocean, Col. poët. 10, 200.—As an honorable designation applied to senators: principes, qui appellati sunt propter caritatem patres,: patres ab honore patriciique progenies eorum appellati,.—Hence, patres = patricii, opp. to plebeii: quā re ad patres censeo revertare: plebeii quam fuerint importuni, vides,: patres conscripti, v. conscribo: pater patrum, pater sacrorum, pater nomimus, the title given to the high-priest of Mithras,; ; ; : patratus, v. h. v. under patro, P. a.—Of the founder of a school: Zeno, pater Stoicorum,; of a teacher, as a source or creator: Isocrates pater eloquentiae,: Herodotus pater historiae,: pater patriae, the father of his country, of Cicero, : quem Q. Catulus, quem multi alii saepe in senatu patrem patriae nominarant,; cf.: Roma patrem patriae Ciceronem libera dixit,.—So of Marius: C. Marium quem vere patrem patriae ... possumus dicere,; of Trajan, and other emperors: at tu etiam nomen patris patriae recusabas,; cf. ; ; ; ; cf. also: pater senatūs,; ; ; ; : pater orbis,; ; .—As a term of respect: pater Aeneas,; esp., to an old man,; ; so .—
In eccl. Lat., the Supreme Being, God: sicut enim Pater habet vitam in semet ipso,: confiteor tibi, Pater Domine caeli et terrae,: Pater caelestis,; : Pater vester qui in caelis est,: Pater noster, qui es in caelis,: adorabunt Patrem,; saep.—*
Pater cenae, the host, : misericordiarum,. —Hence, by way of opposition, *
Pater esuritionum, the father of hunger-pains, said of a very poor man who suffers from hunger, .—
Of animals, sire: virque paterque gregis,; ; .

senses: to disclose, uncover, reveal, bring to light
la:verb:patefacio.html:
pătĕfăcĭo, fēci, factum, 3 (scanned pătēfēcit, ; and in
pass. pătēfīet, ), v. a.
pateo-facio
, to make or lay open, to open, throw open (freq. and class.; syn.: pando, recludo, aperio).
Lit.: iter,: patefacere et munire alicui aditum ad aliquid,: aures assentatoribus,: portas,: ordines, aciem,: sulcum aratro,: oculos,: patefacta triumphis Janua. : iter per Alpes patefieri volebat,; cf. Inscr. Marin. Fratr. Arv. p. 27.—Poet.: postera lux radiis latum patefecerat orbem,i. e. had exposed to view, made visible,.—Esp. (= άνοίγειν), to open the way, as a discoverer or pioneer; to be the first to find: vias,: tellus in longas est patefacta vias,, cf.: patefactumque nostris legionibus Pontum,: loca,.—
Trop., to disclose, expose, detect, bring to light: si hoc celatur, in metu; sin patefit, in probro sum,: odium suum in aliquem,: patefacere verum et illustrare,: rem,: patefacere et proferre aliquid,: veritas patefacta,; : Lentulus patefactus indiciis,convicted,: qui ea proferenda et patefacienda curavit,: se aliquid patefacturam,.

pătĕra, ae, f.
pateo

la:noun:patronus.html:
pā^trōnus, i, m.
pater
.
Lit., a protector, defender, patron (of individuals, or of cities and entire provinces; also, the former master of a freedman); PATRONVS SI CLIENTI FRAVDEM FECERIT SACER ESTO, Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. ; quot enim clientes circa singulos fuistis patronos, tot nunc, etc., Liv 6, 18, 6: ego me patronum profiteor plebis,; civitatum et nationum,; ; cf.: tum conventus ille Capuae, qui me unum patronum adoptavit, etc.,; Inscr. A. U. C. 742, Marin. Fratr Arv. p. 782; see also ; ; sq.: patronus, defensor, custos coloniae,; .—Of the former master of a freedman or freedwoman: volo me placere Philolachi, meo patrono,: civis Romani liberti hereditatem Lex XII. Tabularum patrono defert, si intestato sine suo herede libertus decesserit, Ulp. Fragm. tit. 29, § 1; cf. ; : corrupti in dominos servi, in patronos liberti,.—
Transf., a defender before a court of justice, an advocate, pleader (syn.: advocatus, causidicus, procurator, cognitor): judicis est semper in causis verum sequi, patroni nonnumquam verisimile, etiamsi minus sit verum, defendere,; : patronus alicui causae constitui,; cf.: his de causis ego huic causae patronus exstiti,; Lex. Servil. lin. 9: patronus partis adversae,; cf.: patronus adversarii,; .—
In gen., a defender, advocate: eam legem a vestrorum commodorum patrono esse conscriptam,: foederum ac foederatorum,: justitiae,: qui modo patronus nunc cupit esse cliens,.—Comically:

video ego te, propter malefacta qui es patronus parieti, i. e. standing like a patron in front of the wall (of one who, for fear of blows, places himself with his back to the wall, ; cf. . —As an affectionate and respectful form of address: mi patrone, immo potius mi pater,; .

la:verb:patro.html:
pā^tro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
etym. dub.; prob. from root pat- of pateo, q. v.; cf. Gr. πατος
,
to bring to pass, execute, perform, achieve, accomplish, bring about, effect, finish, conclude (rarely used by Cic., by Cæs. not at all; syn.: conficio, perago, perpetro).
In gen.: ubi sementim patraveris,: conata,: operibus patratis,: promissa,: bellum,to bring the war to an end,; ; ; ; ; cf. : incepta,: facinus,; : consilia,: cuncta,: pacem,to conclude a peace,: jusjurandum, as pater patratus (v. infra),to pronounce the customary form of oath in making a treaty,: jussa,to execute,: patrata victoria,obtained, gained,: patrati remedii gloria,the glory of the effected cure, multas mortes jussu Messalinae patratas, .—
In partic., in mal. part.: patranti fractus ocello. i. e. with a lascivious eye, : sunt lusci oculi atque patrantes,. (Cf., respecting the accessory notion of patrare, .)—Part. perf.: pā^trātus, act. (as if from patror, āri), in the phrase pater patratus, the fetial priest, who ratified a treaty with religious rites: pater patratus ad jusjurandum patrandum, id est sanciendum fit foedus, Liv 1, 24, 6; cf. ; ; .

la:adj:paternus.html:
păternus, a, um, adj.
pater
,
of or belonging to a father, fatherly, paternal (said of the property, possessions, external relations, etc., of a father; while patrius is used of that which belongs essentially to his nature, dignity, or duty; hence, in good prose: patrius amor, animus, patria potestas, patrium jus; but paterni agri, liberi, servi, liberti, etc.).
Lit.: injuria,against the father,: haud paternum istuc dedisti,: horti,: libertus,: bona paterna et avita,: hospitium,: regna,: res,: animus,: paterni animi indoles (a weaker expression than patrii, v. Weissenb. ad loc., and cf. Krebs, Antibarb. p. 833),: irae,: vel paternam vel avitam gloriam consequi,: civitatem paterno consilio florentissimam accipere,: paternum maternumque genus et nomen,. —
Also (acc. to pater, II. B.), ancestral, of or belonging to forefathers (late Lat.): sepulchra paterna,: mos,: traditio, Pet. 1, 18.—
Transf.
Of one's native country: paterni Fluminis ripae,: terra,.—
Of animals, : color,.—
In gram.: casus paternus,the genitive case, P.

senses: to be exposed, revealed, disclosed, vulnerable
to increase or extend (said of frontiers or land)
la:verb:pateo.html:
păteo, ŭi, 2, v. n. root pat. (perh. orig. spat.; cf. spatium); Gr πεταννυμι, πιτνημι, to spread out; πετασμα, curtain; πεταλον, leaf; cf.: patulus, patina; also perh. pando (for pantdo)],
to stand open, lie open, be open.
Lit.: januae, aedes patent,: facite totae plateae pateant,. nares semper propter necessarias utilitates patent, : omnibus haec ad visendum patebant cotidie,: cur valvae Concordiae non patent?: semitae patuerant,: ne fugae quidem patebat locus,: patuere fores,: (fenestrae) sine injuriā patent, et saep. —
In partic.
To lie open, be exposed to any thing: patens vulneri equus,: latus ictui,.—
To stretch out, extend (cf. porrigor): Helvetiorum fines in longitudinem milia passuum CCXL. patebant,; : schoenus patet stadia XL.,.—
Trop.
In gen., to be open, free, allowable, accessible, attainable: si nobis is cursus pateret,: ad quos omnis nobis aditus, qui paene solis patuit, obstructus est,: praemia quae pateant stipendiariis,: ut intellegant omnia Ciceronis patere Trebiano,: alicui, to yield to: lux aeterna mihi ... dabatur, Si mea virginitas Phoebo patuisset amanti,; ; .—
In partic.
Of the hearing, etc., to be open, ready to hear: (constare inter omnis video) patere aurīs tuas querelis omnium,: si cujus aures ad hanc disputationem patent,: meas auris ... omnium praeceptis patuisse. : tamquam nullo magis tempore ad simplices cogitationes pateat animus,: semita Tranquillae per virtutem patet unica vitae,.—
To be exposed or subject to any thing, : longis morbis senectus, acutis adulescentia magis patet,: qui vanus et excors est patebit contemptui,.—
To extend: in quo vitio latissime patet avaritia,: late patet et ad multos pertinet,.—
To be clear, plain, well known, evident, manifest (cf.: appareo, detegor): operta quae fuere, aperta sunt, patent praestigiae,: cum illa pateant in promptuque sint omnibus, etc.,: quod in tabulis patebat,: in adversariis (hoc nomen) patere contendit,.—With subject-clause: cum pateat aeternum id esse, quod, etc.,.—Absol.: quid porro quaerendum est? factumne sit? at constat: a quo? at patet,.—Hence, pă-tens, entis, P. a., open, accessible, unobstructed, passable.
Lit.: caelum ex omni parte patens atque apertum,: campi patentes,.—Comp.: in locis patentioribus,: via patentior,.—
Transf., open, wide: dolium quam patentissimi oris,.—
Trop.
Open, exposed: domus patens, et exposita cupiditati et voluptatibus,: pelagoque volans da vela patenti,: urbs patens,unwalled,.—
Evident, manifest: causa,.—* Adv.: pătenter, openly, clearly; in comp.: patentius et expeditius (opp: implicite et abscondite),

la:verb:patesco.html:
pătesco (-isco), pătŭi, 3,
v. inch. n. [pateo], to be laid open, to be opened, to open (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic.).
Lit.: atria longa patescunt,: portus patescit,: patescens fungus,. —
Transf., to stretch out, extend: paulo latior patescit campus,: neque poterat patescere acies,: civitates, in quas Germania patescit,; ; cf.: latius patescente imperio,.—
Trop., to be disclosed, to become visible, evident, manifest: ratio patescit,: nunc primum certā notitiā patescente,: tum vero manifesta fides Danaumque patescunt Insidiae, (but the true reading, B. and K., is quae res patefecit).

la:noun:patientia.html:
pătĭentĭa, ae, f.
patior
,
the quality of bearing, suffering, or enduring, patience, endurance.
Lit.
In gen.: pati entia est honestatis aut utilitatis causā rerum arduarum ac difficilium voluntaria ac diuturna perpessio,: patientia famis et frigoris,: hominum ea patientia, virtus frugalitasque est,: paupertatis,: audiendi,; .—
In partic., submission to unnatural lust, pathicism, ; ; ; ; and 25; Mos. et Rom. Leg. Coll. 5, 3, 2.—
Transf.
Forbearance, indulgence, lenity: constantiam dico? nescio an melius patientiam possem dicere,: quousque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientiā nostrā?; : quem duplici panno patientia velat,: levius fit patientiā Quicquid corrigere est nefas,.—
In a bad sense, indolence, want of spirit: ne quis in me aut nimiam patientiam, aut nimium stuporem arguat, Porc. Latro ap. ; : in patientiā firmitudinem simulans,.—
Submissiveness, subjection: usque ad servilem patientiam demissus,: Britanniam uno praelio veteri patientiae restituit,; .

pā^trĭmōnĭum, ii, n.
pater
,
an estate inherited from a father, a paternal estate, inheritance, patrimony (syn. hereditas).
Lit.: lauta et copiosa,; : amplum et copiosum,: expellere aliquem e patrimonio,: patrimonio ornatissimo spoliari,: naufragium patrimonii luculentissimi,: patrimonia effundere,: devorare,: eripere patrimonium alicui,: amplificare, prooem. § 7; Aug. Mon. Ancyr. et saep.; ; ; . —
Trop.: in populi Romani patrimonio,: ut plebem tribus suis patrimoniis deleniret,: Mucius quasi patrimonii propugnator sui,inheritance,: paterni nominis,.

From the time of the emperor Constantine, patricius became the title of a person high in office at court, ; .

pā^trŭus, i, m.
pater, like the Sanscr. pitrivya, patruus, from pitri
,
a father's brother, paternal uncle (opp. avunculus, a mother's brother, maternal uncle); cf. .
Lit.: L. Cicero patruus,: tutor et patruus,; : patruus magnus = frater avi,: patruus major = frater proavi,; : major patruus = avi et aviae patruus, Paul. ex Müll.: patruus maximus = frater abavi, ; plur., ; .—
